lesson.title: Can You Trust the T? Checking Conditions for T-Procedures
lesson.summary: T-procedures require a random sample, independent observations, and a population distribution close enough to normal, with the normality requirement relaxing as sample size grows.
lesson.body:
Before trusting a t-interval or, later, a one-sample t-test, three conditions need to be checked. Randomness: the data must come from a random sample or randomized experiment. Independence: when sampling without replacement, the 10 percent condition applies, the sample size should be no more than 10 percent of the population, so individual observations behave as though independent. Normality: the population the sample was drawn from should be approximately normally distributed, or at least not so skewed or outlier-ridden that the sample mean's sampling distribution fails to be approximately normal.

That normality condition is checked differently depending on how much data you have, since a larger sample allows more departure from normality in the population while still producing a nearly normal sampling distribution for the mean, an application of the same central-limit-theorem logic behind assessing normality more generally. As a rough guideline: with a small sample, roughly under 15 observations, use t-procedures only if a graph of the data, like a dotplot or boxplot, shows a roughly symmetric, single-peaked shape with no outliers. With a moderate sample, roughly 15 up to 30, t-procedures are reasonable unless the data show strong skewness or clear outliers. With a large sample, roughly 30 or more, t-procedures can generally be used even when the population distribution is skewed, because the sample mean's own sampling distribution is close to normal regardless, though outliers so extreme they pull the sample mean far off center are still worth flagging.

Applied to the cereal box example from the previous section: the boxes were described as a random sample, satisfying randomness; as long as this production line makes at least 120 boxes, 10 times the sample size of 12, independence is satisfied; and with only 12 boxes, the small-sample guideline applies, so before trusting that 95 percent interval, an inspector should actually look at a graph of the 12 weights to confirm there is no strong skew or outlier. Skipping this step is a common shortcut, but it is exactly the check that keeps a t-interval or t-test meaningful rather than just mechanically correct.
